title: Lattice Configuration Generation with a Self-Learning Diffusion Model
abstract: We show that a diffusion sampler for lattice-field configurations can be trained without preparing training data by an external Monte Carlo calculation. Starting from exactly sampled configurations at $β=0$, we construct a self-bootstrap sampler, SLDiffusion, in which periodic Gaussian proposals with a fixed learned score are Metropolis--Hastings corrected, at each $β$, against the same physical target at every noise level, and only replay configurations from the resulting chain are used to train the score at the next stage. In the two-dimensional compact XY model, self-training proceeds from $β=0.30$ to $0.50$ at $L=4$. At $β=0.5$, the energy and vortex densities for $L=4,6,8,12$ agree with independent Hybrid Monte Carlo calculations within $1.35σ$. Volume-native retraining at $L=8$ and $12$ improves both the proposal displacement and autocorrelation. The integrated autocorrelation times of the energy and vortex densities remain below two for all volumes studied. These results demonstrate that a Metropolis-corrected diffusion sampler can be self-trained without configurations drawn in advance from the target coupling.
summary: This paper introduces SLDiffusion, a novel self-training diffusion sampler designed to generate accurate lattice field configurations without needing pre-existing Monte Carlo data at the target coupling. By bootstrapping training data from its own Metropolis-Hastings corrected chain, it successfully simulates the 2D XY model and matches established results within small statistical errors.
main_problem: Developing a method for generating lattice field configurations that avoids requiring external training data from initial Monte Carlo calculations when using diffusion models.
main_result: The self-learning diffusion sampler (SLDiffusion) successfully estimates physical observables in the 2D XY model, matching independent HMC results within $1.35\sigma$ at $ eta=0.5$.
method: A self-bootstrap mechanism is used where a Markov chain starts from an exactly sampleable distribution ($ eta=0$) and iteratively trains its score network using only configurations replayed from the preceding Metropolis-Hastings corrected chain.

key_observables: Energy density, vortex densities, helicity modulus ($\Upsilon$), and the Schwinger–Dyson temperature ($ eta_{SD}$).
important_parameters: Coupling constant $\beta$ (tested range: $0.30$ to $0.50$) and lattice size $L$ ($4, 6, 8, 12$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the Metropolis-Hastings correction at every noise level preserves the physical invariant distribution ($\pi_{\beta}$), allowing for self-training.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two coupled ladders: the self-bootstrap beta ladder (for training data generation) and the diffusion-noise ladder (which undergoes MH correction at every step).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SLDiffusion framework, details the self-bootstrap process starting from $\beta=0$, presents diagnostics like autocorrelation times and three-way splits to validate chain quality, and concludes by demonstrating convergence to known physical results.
why_interesting: While focused on lattice field theory, the core methodology—using ML models (diffusion) corrected by exact physics constraints (MH acceptance)—is a powerful general technique for simulating complex high-dimensional physical systems where sampling is difficult.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The two ladders in SLDiffusion. The self-bootstrap beta ladder constructs training data from the exact β = 0 distribution by promoting MH-corrected replay. Here Rk is the training replay at βk defined in Eq. (3.3); only R0 is generated directly from the exact β = 0 distribution. The diffusion-noise ladder is the noise schedule within one SLDiffusion -MAALA proposal. Every noise level is MH-corrected against the same physical target; the ladder is not used as unadjusted transport between intermediate noised distributions. Physics measurements are made on an MH-corrected chain with a fixed transition kernel.

Figure 2. Acceptance, MSJD, integrated autocorrelation times, and Schwinger–Dyson temperature along the L = 4 self-bootstrap ladder. Solid lines in the upper panels denote networks retrained at each β; dashed lines denote bridges used to construct replay for the next stage. The lower-left panel shows the two observables for the retrained chains. Autocorrelation-time uncertainties are evaluated using Eq. (2.14).

Figure 3. Score-training diagnostics. Left: maximum improvement of the validation mean squared error (MSE) over noise scales at each β on the L = 4 ladder. Center: loss history at L = 4, β = 0.50. Right: validation MSE improvement at each noise scale for β = 0.5.

Figure 4. Comparison of observables at L = 6, β = 0.5. Error bars show 1σ statistical uncertainties. SLDiffusion-MAALA uses 50,000 measurements and the independent HMC calculation uses 500,000. The smaller HMC uncertainties result from an effective sample size approximately 3.7–3.8 times larger.

Figure 5. Volume dependence of the integrated autocorrelation time at β = 0.5. The left and right panels show the energy and vortex densities, respectively, for SLDiffusion-MAALA and HMC at L = 4, 6, 8, 12. One unit on the horizontal trajectory index corresponds to one saved trajectory of each method. A SLDiffusion-MAALA trajectory contains 32 full- lattice updates, whereas an HMC trajectory has length one. Error bars are evaluated using Eq. (2.14).
